performers: Beatrice Harrison, cello; Symphony Orchestra; Edward Elgar, conductor
question: What survives when a concerto is compressed onto four acoustic sides?
intro: Harrison and Elgar compress all four movements onto four acoustic record sides, issued in 1921. This is an abridgement, not the complete score: follow the cello’s changing role from opening recitative through scherzo and Adagio to the shortened finale.

sections.mNote: side regions are approximate, not bar-aligned movement boundaries

sections.label: Fourth side · shortened finale

cues.title: A concerto on four sides
cues.text: This is the abridged whole concerto, not a sixteen-minute finale. Follow Harrison’s solo line against the orchestral responses, but do not equate the acoustic recording’s balance with the sound a concert audience would have heard.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive description identifies four twelve-inch acoustic sides, Harrison and Elgar, and a separate duration for each movement. The analysis measures this single supplied stream at 952.3 seconds. https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: Speech before song
cues.text: The concerto’s opening contrasts chordal, speech-like writing with a sustained melodic line. Across this abridged first movement, listen for the difference between a gesture that interrupts and a phrase that carries on across the bar.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck’s musical tour describes the solo recitative and subsequent melody. This is a movement-wide distinction, not a timed identification of a retained bar: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Salmond at the première
cues.text: Felix Salmond, not Harrison, gave the first performance on 27 October 1919 at Queen’s Hall, with Elgar conducting the London Symphony Orchestra. Harrison’s first recording session followed in December.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society lists the première personnel and date; the archive supplies the December session: https://www.elgar.org/3cellcon.htm

cues.title: Weight before withdrawal
cues.text: Across this early stretch, the sound gathers weight before falling back. Follow the length of the sustained line through that change rather than treating the strongest attack as the whole phrase.
cues.evidence: The report shows rising relative level from about 1:25 to 2:00, then a marked decline through 2:20. This is a contour within this transfer, not a comparison of orchestral dynamics.

cues.title: The early crest recedes
cues.text: The recorded sound falls back after the first broad crest. Keep the phrase in mind across this withdrawal; the thinner sound is not necessarily a change of subject.
cues.evidence: The analysis falls from −9.4 dB at 1:50 to −25.1 dB at 2:20, remaining quiet at 2:25. It establishes a level contour, not the identity of a theme.

cues.title: Solo and reply
cues.text: Throughout this movement, distinguish the solo line from the orchestral replies. A concerto can develop an argument by changing who carries a phrase, without introducing a new melody each time.
cues.evidence: The work’s solo-orchestral exchange is described in Frank Beck’s musical tour. This general question does not claim a specific handover in the abridged take: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Work at Brinkwells
cues.text: Elgar completed the concerto during the summer of 1919, after the Violin Sonata, String Quartet and Piano Quintet. Alice took the finished score to Fittleworth Post Office on 8 August.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck’s composition history draws on Alice’s diary and the correspondence: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Two sessions, one issue
cues.text: The archive dates three sides to 22 December 1919 and the replacement slow-movement side to 16 November 1920. The year in a recording title therefore cannot describe every session represented by this stream.
cues.evidence: The archive assigns HO 4607-AF to the later session, with the other three matrices in December 1919. Session and release dates are kept separate in the dossier. https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: The scherzo’s short gestures
cues.text: The second movement replaces the first movement’s broad phrases with quick, compact figures. Listen for how much character can reside in an attack or a brief release, rather than in the length of a sustained note.
cues.evidence: The archive identifies the second side as Lento — Allegro molto. Beck describes its darting solo writing; no retained figure is assigned an exact time: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A local rise and fall
cues.text: This stretch gathers weight and then quickly withdraws. The short swell is a different scale of event from the broad first-movement crest: listen for the continuing motion beneath it.
cues.evidence: The report rises to −13.8 dB at 5:25, then falls to −21.9 dB at 5:40. These measurements describe this transfer, not a dynamic marking in the score.

cues.title: Small notes, long direction
cues.text: Through the quick writing, try following a whole phrase rather than counting every short note. The contour can remain clear even when individual attacks merge in the acoustic recording.
cues.evidence: A general listening suggestion for the source-identified Allegro molto. No onset count is treated as a reliable count of cello notes.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One movement per side
cues.text: The four issued sides each hold one movement. The concerto is abridged; their nearly equal playing times do not reproduce the proportions of the complete work.
cues.evidence: The archive lists side durations of 4:00, 3:52, 3:58 and 4:00, alongside the HMV matrices and catalogue numbers. It does not establish that every individual movement contains cuts.

cues.title: Leave room for a pause
cues.text: As the second side draws to its end, listen to the space around the last gestures. The joined digital file cannot reproduce the listener’s original task of stopping and changing a disc.
cues.evidence: The report identifies unusually quiet windows at 7:45 and 7:50 before the third side begins around 7:52. The historical side sequence comes from the archive, not the audio alone.

cues.title: Issued after the sessions
cues.text: HMV issued the first disc, D541, in May 1921 and the second, D545, in June. The four sides are already joined in the archive’s single file; no new concatenation has been made for this edition.
cues.evidence: The source gives both issue months and supplies a single 952.31-second FLAC with an MP3 derivative, alongside photographs of all four labels. https://archive.org/metadata/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: The slow movement’s line
cues.text: The Adagio gives the cello sustained melodic writing rather than a display of fast passagework. Across this side, follow the connection between notes and the accompaniment beneath them; the spaces between phrases are part of the design.
cues.evidence: The archive identifies side three as Adagio; Beck describes its connected lyrical phrases. No note onset or sounding key is inferred from the noisy transfer: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pitch belongs to the transfer
cues.text: The transfer notes report a pitch difference between the later slow-movement side and the other sides, corrected digitally here. Treat changes of colour across the whole stream cautiously: recording and restoration choices sit between the players and this playback.
cues.evidence: The transfer account gives approximately A=435 Hz at 78 rpm for the earlier sides and A=430 Hz for side three before digital adjustment. These are transfer observations, not a verified session tuning. https://archive.org/details/httpsarchive.orgdetailselgar-concerto-for-violoncello-and-orchestra-in-e-minor-op-85-hmv-d-541-545

cues.title: A slow movement swell
cues.text: The slow movement’s quieter line gathers recorded weight in this stretch. Hear the swell as part of an extended phrase, rather than as the arrival of a new fast section.
cues.evidence: After the quieter 9:20 window, level rises at 9:25–9:30 and remains comparatively high around 9:45–9:55. The report cannot establish which orchestral desks contribute.

cues.title: A bass beneath the melody
cues.text: Throughout the slow movement, give some attention to the accompaniment’s lower register. A sustained melody can change its harmonic meaning when the bass moves underneath it.
cues.evidence: A general harmonic listening question for the Adagio; the report’s unstable local-key labels are not published as chords or a reliable account of the recording’s pitch.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The slow side withdraws
cues.text: The third side recedes before the finale’s renewed activity. Compare the space left by the closing slow phrase with the more insistent rhythm that follows.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls across the late third side, with quiet windows at 11:25–11:35 and a pronounced low point at 11:45 before the rise from 11:50.

cues.title: A shortened final movement
cues.text: The last side compresses the finale into roughly four minutes. The comparison isolates a shared early passage rather than stretching this abridgement across the complete modern finale; missing music is not evidence that Elgar simply conducts everything faster.
cues.evidence: The archive lists the finale at four minutes. A quiet region near 11:45 is followed by renewed activity around 11:50 and a strong measured boundary at 11:54; the side marker is approximate.

cues.title: Motion against sustained line
cues.text: The finale sets more assertive rhythmic writing beside the cello’s longer phrases. Across this shortened side, compare those kinds of motion without assuming that every contrast means a new theme.
cues.evidence: Beck describes the finale’s contrast between orchestral assertion and solo digression. The retained bars are not mapped here: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The Colvins’ dedication
cues.text: The concerto is dedicated to Sir Sidney and Lady Frances Colvin, friends of the Elgars. In July 1919 Elgar told Sidney that he had nearly completed a large concerto for violoncello.
cues.evidence: The dedication and the July letter are documented in the Elgar Society’s introduction and Frank Beck’s history: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Line against recorded weight
cues.text: Through this part of the last side, keep following the cello’s phrase when the surrounding sound grows stronger. Changes in prominence need not mean that the soloist changes character: the acoustic balance can also determine which detail survives.
cues.evidence: A general solo-versus-ensemble listening question within the source-identified finale. The report shows strong relative-level windows around 14:05–14:15 but cannot separate the cello from the orchestra.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The later recorded crest
cues.text: This passage reaches one of the transfer’s strongest sustained levels. Follow the phrase across the crest; the sound’s weight alone does not reveal the original orchestral balance.
cues.evidence: The 14:05 and 14:15 windows are among the report’s five loudest, followed by a fall at 14:20. No individual instrumental entry is claimed.

cues.title: A compressed final argument
cues.text: Keep the whole concerto’s contrast of declamation and sustained melody in mind. This side is substantially shortened, so a brief return or interruption cannot be judged by the proportions of a complete modern performance.
cues.evidence: The archive and dossier establish the four-side abridgement. This general listening question does not identify the location or extent of any particular cut.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before the final burst
cues.text: The late passage gives back some of its earlier weight before the short ending. Listen for the difference between the sustained line and the abrupt energy needed to close the disc.
cues.evidence: The report places quieter windows at 15:00–15:15 and 15:30–15:35, before the final rise at 15:40. No exact recall of an earlier theme is assigned to these windows.

cues.title: A final resurgence
cues.text: After the quieter late passage, the recorded sound briefly regains weight before the ending. Compare the duration of that last burst with the preceding withdrawal; this is an ending, not the start of another disc side.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from about −24.6 dB at 15:35 to −11.4 dB at 15:40, then falls to −42.7 dB at 15:50. No exact final chord or instrumental entrance is identified.

transitions.title: A new side changes the gesture
transitions.how: The first movement’s sustained argument gives way to the second movement’s introductory gestures and quick Allegro molto writing. Elgar connects these movements in the concert score, but the historical recording assigns them to separate sides. This digital join therefore combines a change of musical texture with an editorial side change; it is not evidence of an uninterrupted take.
transitions.evidence: The archive’s 4:00 first-side duration places this approximate join. Level falls at 3:55 and renewed activity follows at 4:05–4:20. Frank Beck supplies the change of musical character: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm

transitions.title: Quick figures yield to the Adagio
transitions.how: The quick second movement closes before the Adagio begins. The soloist’s task changes from short articulated figures to a connected melodic line, with accompaniment serving the longer phrase. The transferred side break creates an audible gap; it should not be mistaken for a precisely measured concert pause or for a passage composed between the movements.
transitions.evidence: The archive’s cumulative side durations locate the third side near 7:52. The report’s low 7:45–7:50 level precedes the rise at 7:55. The movement character is documented by Frank Beck, not inferred from machine key estimates.

transitions.title: The slow line meets renewed motion
transitions.how: The Adagio’s sustained phrase gives way to the finale’s stronger rhythmic gestures. In the complete work these movements are connected, but the acoustic issue places the finale on a new side and shortens its argument substantially. Hear the contrast of sustained line and renewed attack without treating the transfer’s gap as part of Elgar’s written transition.
transitions.evidence: The archive lists 4:00 + 3:52 + 3:58 before the finale. The report has a quiet 11:45 window, renewed attacks around 11:50 and a strong 11:54 boundary; 710 s is a passage marker, not a verified first-bar time.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Four acoustic sides, one movement per side; the whole concerto is abridged.
fields.note: This is the abridged whole concerto, not the complete score or a sixteen-minute finale. The supplied stream already joins all four sides. Only a continuous early finale passage is aligned with the complete Skidmore finale; neither complete work durations nor omitted music are equated. The exact cuts and acoustic-session instrumental substitutions are not established, so no modern-score orchestra timeline is projected onto this recording.

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
